scenario: AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

Here’s a breakdown of the key ethical considerations: ### **Key Issues in the Scenario:** 1. **Consent & Autonomy** - Your friend explicitly stated he didn’t want attention or recognition for his actions. Sharing something about him without his consent (especially when he was unreachable) violated his autonomy. Even if his reasons were mixed (self-improvement + volunteering), he had the right to control how his story was shared. - **Your perspective:** You believed he’d be too shy to speak up for himself, but that’s not your call to make. His discomfort suggests he *did* have a preference, even if it wasn’t vocalized. 2. **Intent vs. Impact** - Your intent was likely well-meaning (you wanted to celebrate his work), but the impact was harmful. His reaction—annoyance, withdrawal, and emotional distress—shows that your action crossed a boundary. Even if the post was positive, it still overstepped. - **Key question:** Would he have been okay with it if he’d known? His "no" was clear, but you didn’t ask. 3. **Shyness ≠ Permission** - Just because someone is shy doesn’t mean you can speak for them or share their story without consent. His reluctance to tell others before the trip doesn’t negate his right to privacy afterward. 4. **Timing & Context** - Posting while he was unreachable (and thus unable to respond) is particularly unethical. It’s a power dynamic issue—you had control over the narrative, and he didn’t. 5. **His Reasons for Going** - His claim that he went primarily for self-improvement (not volunteering) is his truth, even if you disagree. Whether his motives were "pure" isn’t for you to judge. His discomfort stemmed from feeling exposed for reasons he didn’t want shared. --- ### **Was It Wrong?** **Yes, it was wrong.** Here’s why: - **Violation of trust:** You betrayed his confidence by sharing something he didn’t want publicized. - **Lack of consent:** Even if you thought you were helping, his "no" was clear (just not in the moment). Respecting boundaries is foundational in relationships. - **Emotional harm:** His reaction (annoyance, withdrawal) shows the post caused him distress. That’s not a "nice thing"—it’s an invasion. --- ### **Why You Might Have Felt Justified:** - You saw an opportunity to "give him recognition." - You assumed his shyness meant he’d never speak up for himself. - You didn’t consider the *how* of sharing—just the *what*. But **ethics isn’t about assumptions or good intentions**; it’s about respecting others’ boundaries, even when they’re quiet about them. --- ### **How to Repair the Relationship:** 1. **Apologize sincerely.** Acknowledge that you overstepped and didn’t respect his wishes. Example: *"I realize now that I didn’t respect your boundaries by posting about your trip. I thought I was helping, but I should’ve asked you first. I’m sorry for making you uncomfortable."* (Avoid excuses like "you were unreachable" or "you’d never tell people.") 2. **Listen to his feelings.** Let him express how it made him feel without interrupting. Validate his emotions, even if you disagree. 3. **Give him space.** He may need time to process. Don’t push for reconciliation too quickly. 4. **Reflect on the lesson.** This is a great opportunity to learn about consent, privacy, and respect in friendships. Moving forward, always ask before sharing about others—even if they’re shy or "wouldn’t say no." --- ### **Final Verdict: <0>** **No, it was not appropriate.** You acted without consent, disregarded his clear (if indirect) wishes, and caused him emotional distress. The right thing would have been to ask him first or wait until he returned to discuss it. --- ### **Bonus Thought:** If you’d asked him *before* the trip, *"Hey, I’d love to help share your volunteer work if you’re comfortable with it,"* he might have said yes. But since you didn’t, you’re responsible for the consequences. This is a teachable moment for both of you.
